observer: AI-assisted visual observer; not a historical-language expert
scope: Geometric layout and object/text adjacency only. No transcription, reading, translation, name, or identity inference.

separation.visibility: Images themselves contain visible script. This is not complete blindness to text. No text was transcribed or read for linguistic content.

coordinates.precision: approximate reading zones; normally tens of pixels, sometimes broader family extents; not glyph segmentation
coordinates.regional_boxes: A broad family rectangle can contain graphics and unrelated text. Consult descriptions. Sample IDs do not imply exhaustive inventory.

conclusions: No unambiguous explicit text-to-object leader was observed in the inspected pages/crops. This is an observation with visibility limits, not a proof that no such line exists anywhere.
page_01: sector boundaries and circular bands dominate; isolated radial strings, multi-line sector blocks, and continuous ring text are different units.

page_02: left/centre scattered motifs supply the strongest single-object adjacency cases; right circle mixes multi-object rows, continuous radial/circular text, compact clusters, and occasional single-object adjacency.
page_03: ten short groups occur in repeated spaces beside descending graphic outlines connected to ten heads and a shared upper structure. One-to-one semantic attachment is uncertain.
Nearest-object matching is not an independent semantic identification. Shared boundaries, rotated text, and interrupted prose can yield false label assignments.
limitations: No exhaustive per-word box inventory or full graphic topology tracing was attempted. All major layout families are covered, with native-crop examples and all ten page_03 middle short groups.
Whole-image views were display-downscaled. Six official native-size crops were additionally inspected; lower portions without crops rely on the whole-image view.
No stroke enhancement, contrast manipulation, rotation, OCR, or generated image reconstruction was used.
Graphic words such as star-shaped, face-bearing, human figure, and tube-like describe visible geometry; they do not establish historical subject identity.
